title: Year 10 English 2026 — Yearly Exam (King Lear + Comparative Essay)
exam_focus: Aligned to the 10ENGB yearly paper: Section 1 is short answer on King Lear extracts (16 questions covering the division of the kingdom and banishment, flattering language, the storm, poor naked wretches, Gloucester's blinding, Edmund/Edgar, Cordelia's death, dramatic irony, hamartia, the blindness motif, power/loss/identity); Section 2 is the TKAMB × Mississippi Burning comparative essay (10 questions: thesis, topic sentences, integrating extracts, comparing techniques, thematic axes, closing the loop); plus 4 general writing-technique questions. Shakespeare quotations have been checked line by line against the MIT Complete Works (shakespeare.mit.edu); only orthography follows that edition.

questions.stem: How does King Lear decide how to divide his kingdom at the start of the play?
options: By giving the largest share to the eldest daughter
By asking each daughter to say how much she loves him
By holding a tournament between the dukes
By drawing lots with his daughters
questions.explanation_en: King Lear asks his three daughters to express their love for him, which will determine their share of the kingdom, making love a measurable performance.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · English(5 multiple choice questions based on the events of your play)

questions.stem: What word does Cordelia use when asked to declare her love, which triggers Lear's rage?
options: Love
Everything
Nothing
Half
questions.explanation_en: Cordelia replies 'Nothing', refusing to use flattery to gain land, and Lear mistakes her honesty for denial, stripping her of her inheritance.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · English

questions.stem: Who is the faithful nobleman banished for speaking in defence of Cordelia, and how does he return?
options: Gloucester, disguised as Poor Tom
Kent, disguised as the servant Caius
Albany, disguised as a knight
Edmund, disguised as a messenger
questions.explanation_en: Kent is banished for defending Cordelia and continues to serve Lear in disguise as Caius, while Poor Tom is Edgar's disguise and Albany is not in disguise.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · English

questions.stem: How does Goneril and Regan's treatment of Lear change after they gain power?
options: They give him more knights than he had before
They reduce the number of knights he may keep, eventually refusing them entirely
They exile him to France
They crown him king of a smaller region
questions.explanation_en: Lear's request to keep 100 knights is reduced to 50 by Goneril and then to 25 by Regan, who eventually refuses to accommodate him, and the removal of his attendants is a key point of humiliation.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · English

questions.stem: Edmund plots against Edgar and Gloucester. Which action most directly sets his plan in motion?
options: He tells Edgar that Gloucester wants him dead, then claims Edgar plotted to kill Gloucester
He openly challenges Edgar to a duel
He reports Edgar to the King
He forges a letter and calls a tournament
questions.explanation_en: Edmund forges letters, tricks Edgar into fleeing, and reports to Gloucester that 'Edgar is plotting against his father', making Edgar a wanted man and himself the legitimate heir.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · English

questions.stem: How does the play end for Lear and Cordelia?
options: They rule the kingdom together
Cordelia is hanged on Edmund's orders and Lear dies of grief with her body
Lear is killed in battle by Albany
They flee to France and survive
questions.explanation_en: Edmund orders Cordelia's execution, and by the time Lear arrives it is too late: he dies holding her body. No happy ending restores order; only Albany and Edgar are left to pick up the pieces.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · English

questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 1 Scene 1:

CORDELIA: Nothing, my lord.
KING LEAR: Nothing!
CORDELIA: Nothing.
KING LEAR: Nothing will come of nothing: speak again.

(a) What does Cordelia's reply reveal about her values? (2 marks)
(b) Explain how Lear's response sets the tragedy in motion. (3 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) 1 mark — Cordelia refuses to flatter or perform love for a reward; she will not compete with her sisters' speeches.
1 mark — her plain 'Nothing' signals honesty and a measured, private love (she loves 'according to my bond'), not an absence of feeling.
(b) 1 mark — Lear equates love with public declaration, so silence is read as rejection.
1 mark — his pun, 'Nothing will come of nothing', shows him thinking in terms of a bargain or debt rather than affection.
1 mark — he banishes Cordelia (and Kent) and divides the kingdom between Goneril and Regan, handing power to the daughters who will destroy him.
questions.explanation_en: The two questions form a causal chain: (a) why Cordelia says 'Nothing' (refusing to perform love, which is a 'duty' not a quote), and (b) linking three points — taking words as love, using puns as transactions, and exile creating a power vacuum.
questions.source: King Lear Act 1 Scene 1 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 1.1); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: States that Cordelia refuses to flatter or perform love for a reward, and will not compete with her sisters' speeches
States that her plain 'Nothing' signals honesty and a measured, private love ('according to my bond' in the answer) rather than an absence of feeling
Explains that Lear equates love with public declaration, so silence is read as rejection
Explains how his pun 'Nothing will come of nothing' shows him thinking in terms of a bargain or debt rather than affection
Explains that he banishes Cordelia and Kent and divides the kingdom between Goneril and Regan, handing power to the daughters who will destroy him

questions.answer:
(a) 1 mark — hyperbole and unverifiable comparison ('more than words can wield', 'dearer than eyesight, space and liberty').
1 mark — a catalogue of absolutes: love is measured against everything (sight, space, liberty, wealth) and therefore means nothing specific.
(b) 1 mark — the contrast with Cordelia's plain 'Nothing' exposes flattery as performance and truth as plain speech.
1 mark — it positions the audience above Lear: we can hear the inflation before he can (dramatic irony).
1 mark — it establishes the play's central error: love treated as language to be counted rather than felt.
questions.explanation_en: This question examines how language is quantified: Goneril uses exaggeration and absolute lists to make love comparable and quotable.
questions.source: King Lear Act 1 Scene 1 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 1.1); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Identifies hyperbole and unverifiable comparison in Goneril's language (e.g. 'more than words can wield', 'dearer than eyesight, space, and liberty')
Identifies her catalogue of absolutes, in which love is measured against everything and therefore means nothing specific
Explains that the contrast with Cordelia's plain 'Nothing' exposes flattery as performance and plain speech as truth
Explains that the speech positions the audience above Lear, who cannot yet hear the inflation (dramatic irony)
Explains that it establishes the play's central error: love treated as language to be counted rather than felt

questions.topic: King Lear · Sight and blindness imagery
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 1 Scene 1:

KENT: See better, Lear; and let me still remain
The true blank of thine eye.

Explain what Kent's image of sight suggests about Lear's error and about the play's wider concerns. (3 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — sight here means judgement or insight, not physical vision: Kent is telling Lear that he is misreading his daughters.
1 mark — Kent offers to be the 'blank' (the true target/centre) of Lear's eye, that is, the honest perspective Lear refuses.
1 mark — the image plants the blindness motif that structures the whole play: Gloucester is literally blinded, and Lear only learns to 'see' once he has lost everything.
questions.explanation_en: 3 marks are given for: sight = judgement (not vision), Kent's voluntary loyalty as a 'target', and this metaphor setting up the blindness theme throughout the play (leading to Gloucester's eye gouging and Lear's eventual loss).
questions.source: King Lear Act 1 Scene 1 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 1.1); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that sight here means judgement or insight rather than physical vision, so Kent is telling Lear that he is misreading his daughters
Explains that Kent offers to be the 'blank' (the true target or centre of Lear's eye), that is, the honest perspective Lear refuses
Explains that the image plants the blindness motif that structures the play, with Gloucester literally blinded and Lear learning to 'see' only after losing everything

questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 1 Scene 1:

LEAR: Come not between the dragon and his wrath.

How does this line help to explain Lear's hamartia? (3 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — the dragon is Lear's self-image: power, terror and untouchability, a king who sees himself as beyond challenge.
1 mark — wrath has replaced judgement: he acts from injured pride rather than reason, and cannot tolerate being contradicted.
1 mark — because this flaw (not fate) drives the banishments and the division of the kingdom, his downfall follows from character, which is what makes the play a tragedy.
questions.explanation_en: Hamartia is not 'bad luck' but a character flaw: Lear's anger overrides his judgement and drives him to expel Cordelia and divide the kingdom. The tragedy is driven by his own character, as the tragic structure requires.
questions.source: King Lear Act 1 Scene 1 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 1.1); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that the dragon is Lear's self-image: power, terror and untouchability, a king who sees himself as beyond challenge
Explains that wrath has replaced judgement, so he acts from injured pride and cannot tolerate being contradicted
Explains that this flaw, not fate, drives the banishments and the division of the kingdom, which is what makes the play a tragedy

questions.topic: King Lear · Power, loss and identity
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 2 Scene 4:

LEAR: I gave you all—
REGAN: And in good time you gave it.

Analyse what this exchange reveals about power, loss and identity. (4 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — Lear still speaks as the giver: his identity is bound up in what he handed over, so he assumes authority continues after the gift.
1 mark — Regan's 'in good time' turns the gift into a completed transaction and cancels his claim on gratitude.
1 mark — the daughters now own the power he thought he kept; the title of king remains but the substance has gone.
1 mark — the play shows identity collapsing when power is transferred: Lear is reduced to 'a poor old man' and has to rebuild a self from bare humanity.
questions.explanation_en: The 4 marks cover three concepts: power has shifted, identity still belongs to the 'giver', and the extract illustrates 'title ≠ substance'. Regan's cold 'in good time' marks the turning point in the power relationship.
questions.source: King Lear Act 2 Scene 4 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 2.4); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that Lear still speaks as the giver, since his identity is bound up in what he handed over and he assumes his authority continues after the gift
Explains that Regan's 'in good time' turns the gift into a completed transaction and cancels his claim on gratitude
Explains that the daughters now hold the power he thought he kept, so the title of king remains but its substance has gone
Explains that identity collapses when power is transferred, leaving Lear a 'poor old man' who must rebuild a self from bare humanity

questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 2 Scene 4:

LEAR: O, reason not the need: our basest beggars
Are in the poorest thing superfluous:

What does this speech reveal about Lear's understanding of need? (3 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — he argues that bare necessity is not enough for human dignity: even beggars have something 'superfluous' beyond survival.
1 mark — he is defending his hundred knights as a symbol of status and respect, not as a practical requirement.
1 mark — the speech shows him reasoning about humanity and hardship, but still from a king's position, so the insight is genuine yet incomplete.
questions.explanation_en: The key to this question is that 'need has two layers': survival needs and human dignity needs. Lear can now speak for the poor, but he still fights for pomp and dignity, which shows that his recognition is incomplete.
questions.source: King Lear Act 2 Scene 4 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 2.4); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that Lear argues bare necessity is not enough for human dignity, since even beggars have something 'superfluous' beyond survival
Explains that he defends his hundred knights as a symbol of status and respect rather than a practical requirement
Explains that the speech shows genuine insight into humanity and hardship but is still spoken from a king's position, so the understanding is incomplete

questions.topic: King Lear · The storm as symbol (3.2)
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 3 Scene 2:

LEAR: Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! rage! blow! ...
I am a man
More sinn'd against than sinning.

(a) How does Shakespeare use the storm symbolically in this scene? (3 marks)
(b) What does 'More sinn'd against than sinning' reveal about Lear's self-knowledge at this point? (3 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) 1 mark — the storm externalises Lear's inner rage and gives his fury a cosmic scale.
1 mark — it is also indifferent nature: wind and rain do not answer him, which cuts human authority down to size.
1 mark — by stripping him of shelter and followers it forces him to confront exposed humanity, preparing the 'poor naked wretches' speech.
(b) 1 mark — he sees himself chiefly as a victim: 'sinn'd against' comes first and carries the weight.
1 mark — he concedes only a lesser share of blame ('more ... than'), so the self-knowledge is partial, not full confession.
1 mark — fuller recognition comes later (Act 4, 'they told me I was every thing; 'tis a lie'), so this scene is a middle stage of his moral journey.
questions.explanation_en: (a) The storm has three functions: externalising anger, showing nature's indifference, and stripping away the facade of power. (b) Note the concessional structure 'more ... than' — he admits fault but portrays himself as a victim, so it's 'partly self-aware', not 'completely repentant'.
questions.source: King Lear Act 3 Scene 2 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 3.2); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that the storm externalises Lear's inner rage and gives his fury a cosmic scale
Explains that the storm is also indifferent nature (wind and rain do not answer him), which cuts human authority down to size
Explains that stripping him of shelter and followers forces him to confront exposed humanity and prepares the 'poor naked wretches' speech
Explains that Lear sees himself chiefly as a victim, with 'sinn'd against' placed first and carrying the weight
Explains that he concedes only a lesser share of blame ('more ... than'), so the self-knowledge is partial rather than a full confession
Explains that fuller recognition comes later (Act 4, 'they told me I was every thing; 'tis a lie'), so this scene is a middle stage of his moral journey

questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 3 Scene 4:

LEAR: Poor naked wretches, wheresoe'er you are,
That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm ...
O, I have ta'en
Too little care of this!

Explain why this speech is a turning point in Lear's moral understanding. (4 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — for the first time he thinks about other people's suffering instead of listing his own injuries.
1 mark — he admits neglect as a ruler: 'too little care of this' is a confession of political and moral failure.
1 mark — the concrete imagery (houseless heads, unfed sides) makes poverty physical rather than abstract, so the audience feels it too.
1 mark — the insight only arrives after he loses power and shelter, so suffering becomes his teacher; the lesson costs him everything.
questions.explanation_en: 4 marks: ① thinking of others' suffering ② acknowledging the ruler's responsibility ③ specific imagery making poverty tangible ④ this awareness is gained through 'losing power'. Don't stop at ① or you'll only get 1 mark.
questions.source: King Lear Act 3 Scene 4 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 3.4); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that for the first time he thinks about other people's suffering instead of listing his own injuries
Explains that he admits neglect as a ruler, so 'too little care of this' is a confession of political and moral failure
Explains that the concrete imagery (houseless heads, unfed sides) makes poverty physical rather than abstract, so the audience feels it too
Explains that the insight only arrives after he loses power and shelter, so suffering becomes his teacher at the cost of everything

questions.topic: King Lear · 'Lendings' and stripping of identity
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 3 Scene 4:

LEAR: Is man no more than this? Consider him well. ...
Off, off, you lendings! come unbutton here.

What does Lear's stripping off his clothes represent? (3 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — 'lendings' treats clothes as borrowed status rather than as part of the self.
1 mark — stripping tests what a human being is when rank, retinue and clothing are removed.
1 mark — it dramatises the play's theme of identity: a king discovers he is only 'a poor, bare, forked animal', which is both a loss and a form of truth.
questions.explanation_en: 3 marks: clothes = borrowed identity, undressing = reducing someone to a 'bare, forked animal', and this action is both loss and awareness. It's better if you can point out the paradox of 'poor, bare, forked animal' (no need to quote verbatim).
questions.source: King Lear Act 3 Scene 4 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 3.4); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that 'lendings' treats clothes as borrowed status rather than as part of the self
Explains that stripping tests what a human being is once rank, retinue and clothing are removed
Explains that the action dramatises the play's theme of identity, since the king discovers he is only 'a poor, bare, forked animal' — both a loss and a form of truth

questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 3 Scene 7:

CORNWALL: Out, vile jelly!
Where is thy lustre now?

(Gloucester has just been bound to a chair and blinded.)

How does Shakespeare make Gloucester's blinding more than physical violence? (4 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — the language ('vile jelly', 'lustre') turns eyes into objects, so the horror is deliberately grotesque rather than heroic.
1 mark — it literalises the blindness motif: Gloucester is punished in his eyes for the moral blindness that let Edmund deceive him.
1 mark — the staging is an abuse of power (a bound guest, a host's authority turned to torture), echoing Lear's abuse of Cordelia and Kent.
1 mark — the audience is forced to watch what the characters refused to see, so the scene makes sight a moral act for the viewer as well.
questions.explanation_en: This question requires explaining 'literal blindness = metaphorical blindness fulfilled': Gloucester loses his eyes due to not seeing Edmund clearly, and the atrocity is a misuse of power, parallel to Lear's banishment of his daughter. If you say 'the audience is forced to see', you can get the 4th mark.
questions.source: King Lear Act 3 Scene 7 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 3.7); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that the language ('vile jelly', 'lustre') turns eyes into objects, making the horror grotesque rather than heroic
Explains that the blinding literalises the blindness motif, punishing in his eyes the moral blindness that let Edmund deceive him
Explains that the staging is an abuse of power (a bound guest tortured by a host's authority), echoing Lear's treatment of Cordelia and Kent
Explains that the audience is forced to watch what the characters refused to see, making sight a moral act for the viewer as well

questions.topic: King Lear · Irony of 'I stumbled when I saw'
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 4 Scene 1:

GLOUCESTER: I have no way, and therefore want no eyes;
I stumbled when I saw ...

Explain the irony in Gloucester's lines. (3 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — when he had eyes he was morally blind, refusing to see Edmund's treachery and turning against Edgar.
1 mark — now that he is physically blind he sees his own errors and Edgar's love, so insight arrives after sight is gone.
1 mark — the paradox 'I stumbled when I saw' states the play's inversion: physical sight and moral vision are opposites, which also describes Lear's journey.
questions.explanation_en: 3 marks: ① having eyes but not seeing the truth ② seeing clearly after becoming blind ③ highlighting the play's 'sight/insight' paradox. It's best to mention the parallel between Gloucester and Lear to show overall understanding.
questions.source: King Lear Act 4 Scene 1 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 4.1); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that when he had eyes Gloucester was morally blind, refusing to see Edmund's treachery and turning against Edgar
Explains that now, physically blind, he sees his own errors and Edgar's love, so insight arrives after sight is gone
Explains that the paradox 'I stumbled when I saw' states the play's inversion of physical sight and moral vision, which also describes Lear's journey

questions.topic: King Lear · Edmund's values and dramatic function
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 1 Scene 2:

EDMUND: Thou, Nature, art my goddess; to thy law
My services are bound.

(a) What does Edmund's address to Nature reveal about his values? (2 marks)
(b) Explain Edmund's dramatic function in the play. (3 marks)
questions.answer:
(a) 1 mark — he rejects the social and legal order (bastardy, custom, inheritance) and claims a 'natural' right instead.
1 mark — his goddess is appetite and self-interest, so 'Nature' becomes an excuse for predation rather than a moral authority.
(b) 1 mark — he is the engine of the plot: the forged letter sets Edgar running and destroys Gloucester's trust.
1 mark — his manipulation exposes other characters' blindness (Gloucester's credulity, Edgar's trust), which doubles Lear's error.
1 mark — his parallel family plot mirrors Lear's, so the two falls together argue that betrayal is a pattern, not an accident.
questions.explanation_en: (a) Edmund uses 'nature' as a goddess to legitimise his desires. (b) Three functions: driving the plot (forging letters), revealing others' 'blindness', and reinforcing the theme through parallel plot. If you mention 'engine of evil' and 'mirror structure', you can get full marks.
questions.source: King Lear Act 1 Scene 2 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 1.2); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that Edmund rejects the social and legal order (bastardy, custom, inheritance) and claims a 'natural' right instead
Explains that his goddess is appetite and self-interest, so 'Nature' becomes an excuse for predation rather than a moral authority
Explains that he is the engine of the plot, since the forged letter sets Edgar running and destroys Gloucester's trust
Explains that his manipulation exposes other characters' blindness (Gloucester's credulity, Edgar's trust), which doubles Lear's error
Explains that his parallel family plot mirrors Lear's, so the two falls together argue that betrayal is a pattern rather than an accident

questions.topic: King Lear · The forged letter and dramatic irony
questions.stem:
Section 1 — scene description (no quotation):

In Act 1 Scene 2 Edmund shows his father Gloucester a letter that he has forged in Edgar's handwriting. He then warns Edgar that their father is furious with him and advises him to arm himself and flee.

Explain how Shakespeare creates dramatic irony here and why it matters. (3 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — the audience watches Edmund stage both sides of the deception, so we know Edgar is innocent while Gloucester believes the letter.
1 mark — each character then acts on information the audience knows to be false, so their choices look like self-destruction.
1 mark — the gap between audience and characters turns the plot into a demonstration of how easily 'sight' (evidence, trust) can be manufactured.
questions.explanation_en: The marking points for dramatic irony are: the audience sees Edmund playing two scenes → characters act on false information → this proves 'seeing/trusting' can be fabricated. For the 3rd mark, you need to elevate to the theme level, not just retell the plot.
questions.source: Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage (Act 1 Scenes 1–3 questions and practice extracts)

criteria.t: Explains that the audience watches Edmund stage both sides of the deception, so we know Edgar is innocent while Gloucester believes the letter
Explains that each character then acts on information the audience knows to be false, so their choices look like self-destruction
Explains that the gap between audience and characters turns the plot into a demonstration of how easily 'sight' (evidence and trust) can be manufactured

questions.topic: King Lear · The gods and the human condition
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 4 Scene 1:

GLOUCESTER: As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods;
They kill us for their sport.

What view of the gods and of human agency does this image express, and how does it fit the play's tragic vision? (4 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — the gods are 'wanton boys': careless, playful and not just, so divine authority is emptied of moral purpose.
1 mark — humans are flies: small, disposable and without control over their fate.
1 mark — the image reverses Gloucester's earlier confidence that the gods are just, and it answers Lear's repeated appeals to the heavens.
1 mark — the play leaves the question open: the innocent die (Cordelia) while the guilty partly escape, so the ending refuses to console the audience with divine justice.
questions.explanation_en: 4 marks: ① gods are portrayed as unjust ② humans are like flies (powerless) ③ this contrasts with Gloucester's earlier belief that 'the gods are just' and responds to Lear's appeal to the gods ④ the ending (Cordelia's death) leaves the 'moral order' in question, highlighting the tragic nature.
questions.source: King Lear Act 4 Scene 1 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 4.1); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that the gods are 'wanton boys' — careless, playful and not just — so divine authority is emptied of moral purpose
Explains that humans are flies: small, disposable and without control over their fate
Explains that the image reverses Gloucester's earlier confidence that the gods are just, and answers Lear's repeated appeals to the heavens
Explains that the play leaves the question open, since the innocent Cordelia dies while the guilty partly escape, so the ending refuses the consolation of divine justice

questions.topic: King Lear · Cordelia's death and poetic justice
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 5 Scene 3:

LEAR: She's gone for ever!
I know when one is dead, and when one lives;
She's dead as earth. ...
Do you see this? Look on her, look, her lips,
Look there, look there!

Why does Cordelia's death make the ending hard to read as poetic justice? (5 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — poetic justice would reward Cordelia's loyalty and punish the guilty in proportion, restoring a moral order.
1 mark — instead the innocent daughter is hanged on Edmund's order, and the reprieve arrives too late to save her.
1 mark — Lear's hard-won sight is rewarded only with her corpse: insight and loss arrive at the same moment.
1 mark — his final 'Look there, look there!' is ambiguous — he may die believing she lives — so the audience is denied a clear consolation.
1 mark — the deaths of Lear and Cordelia withhold the comfort of a restored order, which is why the ending feels unbearable rather than just.
questions.explanation_en: 5 marks are: defining poetic justice → innocent people are killed and rescue comes too late → awareness and loss happen simultaneously → the final lines are ambiguous and offer no comfort → order is not restored, so the sense of 'injustice' is intentional. When answering, you must first define 'what is poetic justice', or you won't have a standard for comparison.
questions.source: King Lear Act 5 Scene 3 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 5.3); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Defines poetic justice as the reward of loyalty and the punishment of the guilty in proportion, restoring a moral order
Explains that the innocent daughter is hanged on Edmund's order and the reprieve arrives too late to save her
Explains that Lear's hard-won sight is rewarded only with her corpse, so insight and loss arrive at the same moment
Explains that his final 'Look there, look there!' is ambiguous (he may die believing she lives), so the audience is denied clear consolation
Explains that the deaths of Lear and Cordelia withhold the comfort of a restored order, which is why the ending feels unbearable rather than just

questions.topic: King Lear · 'I am not ague-proof' and change
questions.stem:
Section 1 — King Lear, Act 4 Scene 6:

LEAR: They told me I was every thing; 'tis a lie, I am not ague-proof.

What does this line show about Lear's changed identity? (4 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — he recalls being told he was 'everything': flattery had built a false, unlimited self.
1 mark — 'tis a lie' is an explicit act of self-correction, spoken by the king about his own former image.
1 mark — 'not ague-proof' means his body is as vulnerable as anyone's, so he now defines himself as a mortal man.
1 mark — the line therefore shows loss producing a truer identity, not simply destroying one, which is central to the play's ending.
questions.explanation_en: 4 marks: ① being flattered into 'omnipotence' ② self-denial ③ confirming human vulnerability through physical weakness (ague = malaria) ④ thus 'loss' also brings a more realistic self. The last mark is at the theme level, don't miss it.
questions.source: King Lear Act 4 Scene 6 (quote: Shakespeare, King Lear 4.6); Section 1 · King Lear short answer — exam format per LEEDER 10ENGB Homepage

criteria.t: Explains that he recalls being told he was 'every thing', so flattery had built a false, unlimited self
Explains that describing that image as a lie ('tis a lie) is an explicit act of self-correction, spoken by the king about his own former image
Explains that 'not ague-proof' means his body is as vulnerable as anyone's, so he now defines himself as a mortal man
Explains that the line shows loss producing a truer identity rather than simply destroying one, which is central to the play's ending

questions.stem: Section 2 asks: 'How do Lee and Parker expose systemic racism?' Which thesis best answers the question?
options: Both texts show that racism is a serious problem in America and that it damages the lives of ordinary people in small towns across the country.
Both Lee and Parker show racism as a system that shields the guilty, but Lee builds a child's slow awareness while Parker forces the viewer to watch.
Lee's novel is more effective than Parker's film because a novel can explain what characters are thinking, while a film can only show what they do.
Parker relies on music and camera angles to create meaning, while Lee relies on first-person narration and on dialogue between the characters.
questions.explanation_en: A good thesis should: cover two texts, provide a controversial argument (racism is 'an institution that protects the guilty'), and forecast the comparison angle (child's perspective vs forced watching). The other options are just general discussions, evaluating merits, and listing techniques without an argument.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — thesis and introduction (10ENGA unit overview; LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline)

questions.topic: Comparative essay · Function of topic sentences
questions.stem: What is the main job of a topic sentence in a comparative body paragraph?
options: To introduce the paragraph by naming the text and the technique it will discuss
To provide a quotation from each text and explain what happens in that scene
To state a comparative claim about both texts that answers part of the essay question
To summarise the plot of both texts so the reader can follow the argument
questions.explanation_en: A topic sentence = the comparative argument this paragraph aims to prove, which must cover both texts and respond to the question. 'To introduce the paragraph by naming the text and the technique it will discuss' is just a signpost, not an argument. 'To provide a quotation from each text and explain what happens in that scene' is evidence. 'To summarise the plot of both texts so the reader can follow the argument' is just retelling.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — body paragraph structure (TKAMB BP1/BP2/BP3 scaffolds)

questions.stem: Write a thesis statement for the question: 'How do Lee and Parker represent the failure of justice?' (4 marks)
questions.answer:
Model answer: 'Lee and Parker both show justice failing because the community closes ranks around its own, yet Lee traces that failure through a child's gradual recognition while Parker makes the viewer complicit in seeing it.'
1 mark — names both composers/texts.
1 mark — makes one arguable claim about the failure of justice.
1 mark — signals the comparative angle (how the two composers differ in method).
1 mark — uses the question's key term ('failure of justice') rather than drifting into a general statement about racism.
questions.explanation_en: To score well you must cover four points: discuss both texts, present a debatable argument, explore comparative angles, and address the keywords of the question.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — thesis writing (LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline: comparative essay, 20 marks)

criteria.t: Names both composers/texts (Lee and Parker)
Makes one arguable claim about the failure of justice
Signals the comparative angle, showing how the two composers differ in method
Uses the question's key term 'failure of justice' rather than drifting into a general statement about racism

questions.stem: You want to use one line from the supplied extract in a body paragraph. Which approach integrates it most effectively?
options: Quote only the few words that carry the technique, then analyse how they shape meaning in the whole text.
Quote the whole extract so the marker can see you have read it, then explain what it means.
Paraphrase the extract without quoting, because quotations take up too much of your word count.
Quote the line, then say that it shows the theme of justice without explaining how the words create that effect.
questions.explanation_en: Integration means embedding short quotes into your own sentences, analysing how the language creates meaning, and linking it back to the whole text and question. Copying a whole paragraph is just repetition, paraphrasing alone loses the language evidence, and quoting without analysis earns no analysis marks.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — integrating the supplied extract (LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline, 20 marks)

questions.topic: Comparative essay · Using the supplied extract
questions.stem: Section 2 requires you to integrate the extract you are given. Explain what this means in practice, and what you should avoid. (4 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — quote selectively: a few words that carry the technique or idea you need.
1 mark — analyse the wording itself (connotation, syntax, imagery) and link it explicitly to the question.
1 mark — connect the extract to the rest of the text, so the extract is a starting point rather than the whole evidence.
1 mark — avoid long quotation, mentioning the extract only in the introduction, or turning the extract into plot summary.
questions.explanation_en: The four scoring points are: quote → analyse language → link to whole text → avoid 'copying a whole paragraph/only mentioning at the start/just retelling the plot'. This is where Section 2 students often lose marks, as the marking criteria clearly state 'integrate the extract'.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — extract integration (LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline)

criteria.t: Explains that integration means quoting selectively, using a few words that carry the technique or idea needed
Explains that it means analysing the extract's wording (connotation, syntax, imagery) and linking it explicitly to the question
Explains that the extract must be connected to the rest of the text, so it is a starting point rather than the whole evidence
Identifies what to avoid: long quotation, mentioning the extract only in the introduction, or turning it into plot summary

questions.stem: Which option states a genuine point of comparison between Lee's novel and Parker's film?
options: Lee's novel has chapters and a narrator, while Parker's film has scenes and actors who speak dialogue.
Lee controls what Scout notices and when she understands it, while Parker controls what the camera shows and when the viewer sees it.
Lee's novel is set in the 1930s and Parker's film is set in the 1960s, so the film is more historically accurate than the novel.
Lee uses words to describe things and Parker uses pictures, which means the film is easier to understand.
questions.explanation_en: Effective comparison focuses on 'how the authors control information and the reader's response': Lee uses Scout's limited perspective to delay understanding, while Parker uses camera angles and editing to control what the audience sees. Saying 'Lee's novel has chapters and a narrator, while Parker's film has scenes and actors' just states the difference in medium, and doesn't constitute a comparison point.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — comparing literary and film techniques (10ENGA film study: visual storytelling, cinematography, director's purpose)

questions.stem: Which pair of moments best supports the claim that both texts show the law failing?
options: Scout narrates the trial from the gallery, and the film's opening shows two water fountains side by side in the street.
The novel criticises the town's gossip about Boo Radley, and the film criticises the way the agents speak to local people.
Tom Robinson is convicted despite Atticus's defence, and the film's inquiry begins only because local police are implicated.
The novel shows a young child learning about her neighbours, and the film shows two agents slowly learning about a small town.
questions.explanation_en: Evidence of 'legal failure' must directly relate to the justice system: Tom being found guilty, and the local law enforcement being involved in the case, requiring federal intervention. Other options discuss perspective, rumour, or 'learning about the town', which don't prove legal failure.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — theme axis: the law fails (10ENGA unit overview; film study context)

questions.stem: Which claim best fits the theme of individual responsibility in both texts?
options: Both texts place responsibility on individuals who let prejudice pass unchallenged, not only on the law.
Both texts place responsibility on the law alone, since individuals cannot be held accountable for prejudice.
Both texts place responsibility on families, since children learn prejudice at home and not in public.
Both texts place responsibility on the main characters, since the wider community is never shown to be at fault.
questions.explanation_en: Individual responsibility means ordinary people who condone prejudice are also responsible, and responsibility isn't just limited to institutions. Saying 'both texts place responsibility on the law alone' or 'on families' or 'on the main characters' goes against the theme of both works.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — theme axis: individual responsibility (10ENGA unit overview)

questions.stem: Plan one comparative body paragraph for the question: 'How do Lee and Parker expose systemic racism?' Give a topic sentence, one textual point from each text, and the comparison you would draw. (5 marks)
questions.answer:
1 mark — a topic sentence naming both texts and making a comparative claim (e.g. both expose a town that protects its own).
1 mark — a specific point from Lee's novel: the trial and the town's hierarchy, with the technique that carries it (Scout's limited narration; the courtroom as a stage).
1 mark — a specific point from Parker's film: for example the opening water-fountain sequence, with the technique that carries it (mid shot, framing, juxtaposition).
1 mark — a comparison sentence explaining how the two methods differ in effect (delayed recognition vs immediate visual exposure).
1 mark — a link back to the question's key term 'systemic', showing what the comparison proves.
questions.explanation_en: For 5 points, you need: a topic sentence (including both texts and comparative argument) → Lee's evidence and technique → Parker's evidence and technique → comparative sentence (effect difference) → conclusion on 'institutional'. Note that both sides need evidence with technique, and just stating the plot won't get you analysis marks.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — paragraph planning (TKAMB BP scaffolds + film deconstruction lessons)

criteria.t: Writes a topic sentence that names both texts and makes a comparative claim (e.g. both expose a town that protects its own)
Gives a specific point from Lee's novel with the technique that carries it (e.g. the trial and the town's hierarchy; Scout's limited narration; the courtroom as a stage)
Gives a specific point from Parker's film with the technique that carries it (e.g. the opening water-fountain sequence; mid shot, framing, juxtaposition)
Includes a comparison sentence explaining how the two methods differ in effect (delayed recognition versus immediate visual exposure)
Links back to the question's key term 'systemic', showing what the comparison proves

questions.stem: Which conclusion best completes a comparative essay without simply repeating the introduction?
options: The comparison matters because Lee's slow recognition and Parker's forced witness demand different responses, so empathy must become action.
In conclusion, both Harper Lee and Alan Parker show that racism is bad, and this is why the two texts are still studied in schools today.
In conclusion, this essay has discussed characterisation, setting and narrative in To Kill a Mockingbird and Mississippi Burning as I set out.
In conclusion, Lee's novel and Parker's film are both important texts that teach readers and viewers about the dangers of prejudice.
questions.explanation_en: The conclusion should 'recap the argument and take it further': discussing how the comparison leads to different moral demands on the reader/audience (empathy must lead to action), rather than just restating the argument. The other options are vague evaluations, retelling the structure, or just repeating 'opposing prejudice'.
questions.source: Section 2 · Comparative essay — conclusion (LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline: integrate the extract, sustain the argument)

questions.stem: Which sentence analyses rather than describes?
options: The camera holds both fountains side by side, so segregation becomes an ordinary arrangement the viewer absorbs before judging it.
In the opening scene Parker shows two water fountains, one for white people and one for black people, standing in the street.
Parker uses a mid shot in the opening scene, and a mid shot is a camera shot taken from a medium distance.
The scene is effective because it shows the audience that segregation really existed in towns in America at that time.
questions.explanation_en: Analysis sentences should have 'technique → effect → impact on the audience' in three steps: the camera angle makes segregation seem like a 'normal arrangement', making the audience accept before judging. Simply retelling the content, defining terms, or making vague assertions won't suffice.
questions.source: Writing skills · Analytical vs descriptive sentences (Term 3 weeks 8–10: refining analytical writing)

questions.stem: What does it mean to 'use' the extract supplied with an essay question?
options: Copying the extract into your essay so the marker knows you have read the question.
Quoting a few words from the extract inside your own sentence and analysing their effect.
Mentioning that the extract exists and then writing about the rest of the text only.
Summarising the extract in your own words without discussing its language.
questions.explanation_en: 'Using' the extract means embedding it as evidence: quoting, analysing language, and linking back to the question and whole text. Copying a whole paragraph, only mentioning at the start, or just paraphrasing don't count as integration.
questions.source: Writing skills · Using the supplied extract (LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline, Section 2 criteria)

questions.stem: Write one comparative topic sentence for a paragraph arguing that both texts show communities protecting their own. (3 marks)
questions.answer:
Model answer: 'Both Lee's Maycomb and Parker's Mississippi town close ranks to protect the people who belong, and each composer shows that protection turning into complicity.'
1 mark — names both texts/communities.
1 mark — states one comparative claim that answers the question (protection becomes complicity).
1 mark — signals the comparison of method or effect rather than just listing two facts.
questions.explanation_en: For 3 points, you need to discuss both texts, have a comparative argument (protection → complicity), and forecast comparative angles. Simply stating 'both have community' is parallel, not comparative, and will only get you 1 point.
questions.source: Writing skills · Topic sentences for comparative paragraphs (TKAMB BP scaffolds)

criteria.t: Names both texts/communities (Lee's Maycomb and Parker's Mississippi town)
States one comparative claim that answers the question (protection becomes complicity)
Signals the comparison of method or effect rather than just listing two facts

questions.stem: Why does a comparative essay need a comparative topic sentence in every body paragraph?
options: Because the examiner only reads the first sentence of each paragraph when marking the essay.
Because the introduction cannot mention either text and the body must do it instead.
Because quotations from two texts must appear in the same sentence for the essay to count.
Because the argument must run across both texts, so every paragraph has to keep both in view.
questions.explanation_en: Comparison essay marks come from 'sustained comparative argument throughout the text', so every paragraph's topic sentence should cover both texts and advance the argument. The other options are incorrect statements about marking or format.
questions.source: Writing skills · Comparative topic sentences (LEEDER 10ENGB exam outline: comparative essay, 20 marks)
